title: Meal Prep on a Budget
learning_objectives: Plan weekly meals with dietary constraints and a budget
Adapt meals to what's on sale

events.description: You have $50 for a week of meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner). That's about $2.38 per meal. The store has chicken thighs on sale ($2/lb instead of $5/lb), eggs are $3/dozen, rice is $1/lb, and seasonal vegetables are $2/lb. How do you approach your shopping list?

choices.label: Build meals around what's on sale
choices.effect: Smart! Buying 3 lbs of chicken ($6 instead of $15) frees up $9 for other ingredients. Sale shopping stretches your budget.

choices.label: Plan 3 base recipes that make 7+ servings each
choices.effect: Batch cooking! A big pot of chili, a sheet pan of chicken, and a rice-and-bean mix covers most of the week.

choices.label: Ensure each day hits protein, fiber, and vitamin targets
choices.effect: Nutrition-first planning! You map out daily protein (50g+), fiber (25g+), and varied vegetables before choosing recipes.

events.description: You've planned your meals but realize you're $8 over budget at $58. What do you cut without sacrificing nutrition?

choices.label: Swap 2 chicken dinners for bean-based meals (save $6)
choices.effect: Beans cost 1/3 the price of chicken with similar protein! Chili and bean tacos are delicious AND budget-friendly.

choices.label: Switch fresh veggies to frozen for 3 meals (save $4)
choices.effect: Frozen vegetables are nutritionally identical to fresh and cost 30-50% less! Flash-frozen at peak nutrition.

choices.label: Repeat lunches all week instead of 5 different ones (save $5)
choices.effect: Same lunch 5 days saves prep time AND money. Batch cooking one lunch recipe is wildly efficient.

events.description: Meal prep Sunday! You have 3 hours to cook for the week. How do you organize your time? You're making chicken stir-fry, chili, overnight oats, and prepping salad ingredients.

choices.label: Chili simmers while you stir-fry and prep oats
choices.effect: Parallel cooking! Chili takes 45 min hands-off time — perfect for making other dishes simultaneously. Done in 2 hours!

choices.label: One recipe at a time, clean as you go
choices.effect: Organized and methodical! Takes the full 3 hours but your kitchen stays clean and nothing burns.

choices.label: Chop ALL vegetables first, then cook everything
choices.effect: Mise en place! Pro chefs prep first. Once everything is chopped, cooking goes lightning fast.

events.description: Wednesday: your roommate ate some of your prepped meals. You're 3 meals short for the rest of the week with $5 left. What do you do?

choices.label: Raid the pantry — rice, beans, and eggs = 3 meals for $2
choices.effect: Pantry staples to the rescue! Egg fried rice, bean and rice bowl, and scrambled eggs with toast. Under budget!

choices.label: Ask roommate to cover those meals or replace them
choices.effect: Setting boundaries about shared food! Your roommate buys you replacement groceries. Communication works!

choices.label: Add rice/bread to remaining meals to make them stretch
choices.effect: Adding cheap carbs to existing meals extends them. Not ideal nutritionally for every meal, but solves the immediate problem.

events.description: End of week review: How did your $50 meal plan work out? What would you change next week?

choices.label: I need more variety — eating the same thing gets old
choices.effect: Sauce and seasoning variety! Same base ingredients with different seasonings = different meals. Thai one night, Mexican the next.

choices.label: More prep on Sunday so weekday meals are grab-and-go
choices.effect: Pre-portioned containers make busy days effortless. 30 more minutes of Sunday prep saves hours during the week.

choices.label: This week was tight — I'll try $55 next week and see the difference
choices.effect: An extra $5 adds 2-3 more meal options. Sometimes a small budget increase makes a big quality-of-life difference.

recap_template: You meal-prepped for a whole week on $50! You balanced nutrition, budget, time, and dealt with surprises. These are essential skills for living independently.
positive_framing_rules: Never suggest the student is eating poorly or going hungry
Frame budget constraints as creative cooking challenges
Use 'energy and nutrition' language, not calorie restriction
ai_variation_allowed: Change the specific meals and ingredients
Vary the budget amount and sale items

title: Diet + Fitness Planner
learning_objectives: Align nutrition with physical activity goals
Plan meals that support athletic performance

events.description: You're training for [sport] and want to optimize your nutrition. Your coach says you need more protein for muscle recovery and complex carbs for energy. Currently you eat about 60g protein/day. Athletes your age need 80-100g. How do you increase protein?

choices.label: Add protein-rich foods: Greek yogurt, chicken, eggs, beans
choices.effect: Whole food protein! A Greek yogurt at breakfast (+15g), chicken at lunch (+25g), and you're already at 100g. No supplements needed.

choices.label: Focus on protein timing — 20-30g within 30 min of training
choices.effect: Nutrient timing matters! Post-workout protein helps muscles recover faster. A protein-rich snack after practice is key.

choices.label: Track current intake for 3 days first, then adjust
choices.effect: Data-driven approach! You might be eating more protein than you think. Track before you change.

events.description: Game day nutrition: you have a big match at 2 PM. What do you eat and when?

choices.label: Big pasta dinner night before, banana + toast at 11 AM
choices.effect: Classic carb-loading! Complex carbs the night before fill glycogen stores. Light carbs 3 hours before game time provide quick energy.

choices.label: Normal meals but extra hydration starting the morning
choices.effect: Hydration is often more important than food changes! Starting water early ensures you're not dehydrated at game time.

choices.label: Light breakfast, moderate lunch at 11 AM, nothing heavy after
choices.effect: Eating 3+ hours before avoids heaviness during play. A balanced lunch at 11 gives time to digest before your 2 PM game.

events.description: You've been training hard all week and your body feels sore and tired. Your coach says tomorrow is a rest day. What does recovery nutrition look like?

choices.label: Foods that reduce inflammation: berries, fish, leafy greens
choices.effect: Anti-inflammatory foods support recovery! Omega-3s from fish and antioxidants from berries help your body repair.

choices.label: Extra sleep + extra water — let your body do its thing
choices.effect: Rest and hydration are the #1 recovery tools! Your body repairs most during sleep.

choices.label: Same nutrition as training days — your body is still working
choices.effect: Correct insight! Muscles repair on rest days, so they still need protein and nutrients. Don't cut calories on rest days.

events.description: Mid-season: you're tempted to try a restrictive diet trend that a teammate says gives them 'more energy.' It cuts out entire food groups. What do you do?

choices.label: Research the science — does it have evidence?
choices.effect: Critical thinking! Most trendy diets lack evidence for athletes. Peer-reviewed research > social media claims.

choices.label: Ask your coach or a sports nutritionist
choices.effect: Expert advice! A nutritionist explains that restricting food groups can actually decrease performance. Variety is key.

choices.label: Stick with your balanced plan — it's working
choices.effect: If your energy, recovery, and performance are good, why change? Consistency beats trendy diets every time.

recap_template: You built a nutrition plan that supports your athletic training! You learned about protein timing, game-day nutrition, recovery eating, and how to evaluate diet trends with critical thinking.
positive_framing_rules: Never promote restrictive eating or body image concerns
Frame nutrition as fuel and recovery, not weight management
ai_variation_allowed: Change the sport and specific nutritional needs

title: Cooking for One
learning_objectives: Plan meals for a single person efficiently
Reduce food waste with smart shopping
Build basic cooking skills from scratch

events.description: You've just moved out and need to cook for yourself. Recipes for 1 person are rare — most make 4+ servings. How do you handle this?

choices.label: Cook full recipes, freeze portions for later
choices.effect: Freezer meals! Cook once, eat four times. Sunday's chili becomes Monday's lunch and Wednesday's dinner.

choices.label: Learn to halve recipes — smaller batches, less waste
choices.effect: Recipe math! Halving means you need half of everything. Some recipes scale down better than others.

choices.label: Cook components (rice, protein, veggies) and mix differently
choices.effect: Versatile! Grilled chicken becomes salad topping Monday, stir-fry Tuesday, and wraps Wednesday. Same protein, three meals.

events.description: Food waste challenge: you bought a head of lettuce, but one person can't eat it all before it wilts. Bananas are turning brown. Half an onion is left from Tuesday's recipe. How do you reduce waste?

choices.label: Plan the next 2 days' meals around what's about to expire
choices.effect: Salad tonight, banana smoothie tomorrow morning! Planning around what you have prevents waste and saves money.

choices.label: Freeze the bananas, make croutons from stale bread
choices.effect: Preservation skills! Frozen bananas make great smoothies. Brown bananas are perfect for banana bread.

choices.label: Next time: buy smaller quantities even if unit price is higher
choices.effect: For one person, buying less at a higher unit price can actually save money if you throw less away. Waste costs more than the price difference!

events.description: You're tired after work and tempted to order delivery ($15-20) instead of cooking. This has happened 3 times this week. At $15-20/meal vs $3-5 cooking, that's $30-45 extra per week. How do you build a sustainable cooking habit?

choices.label: Find 5 meals you can make in under 15 minutes
choices.effect: Speed recipes! Eggs and toast (5 min), pasta with jarred sauce (12 min), quesadillas (8 min). When cooking is fast, delivery loses its appeal.

choices.label: Sunday prep: chop veggies, marinate protein, cook grains
choices.effect: Weekday cooking drops to assembly! When ingredients are ready, a meal takes 10 minutes instead of 40.

choices.label: Allow delivery once a week, cook the rest — compromise
choices.effect: Realistic! One delivery a week is a treat, not a habit. $15/week on delivery vs $100+ is a huge difference.

events.description: After a month of cooking for yourself, what have you learned?

choices.label: I can actually cook! It gets easier with practice
choices.effect: Cooking confidence! Your first month's meals were simple, but you're already trying new things. Skills compound!

choices.label: Cooking saves so much money — I can see it in my budget
choices.effect: Cooking at home averages $3-5/meal vs $12-20 eating out. Over a year, that's thousands saved!

choices.label: I feel better physically when I control what I eat
choices.effect: Cooking your own food means knowing exactly what's in it. More vegetables, less sodium, and portions that match your needs.

recap_template: You learned to cook for one! Batch cooking, reducing waste, building quick recipes, and creating sustainable habits are the building blocks of feeding yourself for life.
positive_framing_rules: Never shame ordering delivery or eating out
Frame cooking as a skill that develops over time
Celebrate progress from any starting point
ai_variation_allowed: Change the specific recipes and challenges
Vary the budget and dietary preferences
